doc.title: Steve Buckingham, interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 25, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]

title: His course on R&B and segregation, and James Brown's band
summary: He teaches a course on how R&B tore down segregation, recalls his band backing black artists and seeing James Brown's and Ray Charles' big bands.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That’s good info. Well I’ve got to get in a thing about — I know you’re passionate about black music and how it affected bringing the races together.

I taught a course at Vanderbilt for eight years, it’s called Rhythm & Blues Tore Down the Walls of Segregation. I’m teaching it now at Virginia/Wesleyan in Virginia Beach where © Fillius Jazz Archive -18-

I live now. I taught it at Vanderbilt for eight years. But yeah, very passionate about that. Because I lived through it in the 60s. My band in Richmond, we became a really popular back-up band for black artists. Back then there were very few artists that carried bands. James Brown had his big 18 piece band and they were like a machine. I get chills just thinking about that, when I first saw that 18 piece, that curtain open up and those guys are in tuxedos. You know. Three drummers, two guitarists, bass player, an organ player, and then everything else was brass and reeds all across the stage in tuxedos. Not just playing but doing the choreography and the whole thing. And then he hits the stage and it’s a three hour another world. Ray Charles is one of the ones that had a big 18 piece band, the Ray Charles Orchestra with the Raelettes singing background. Again, that was an experience. But very few black artists could afford that. Like when we played with the Drifters, they brought a guitarist with them from New York — I can’t remember his — I don’t know his name, but he was phenomenal. But I was playing the second guitar behind him. Jackie Wilson, no band. We just had the charts and we would back the Impressions. Curtis Mayfield was a great guitarist and producer and writer and singer and a great guy, a gentleman. I played second guitar behind Curtis Mayfield, but most black groups, Jackie Wilson, Otis Redding, occasionally Otis would have a band, they would augment it with some of us, and in Virginia and the Carolinas we became like one of the key what, they called it, back-up bands.
